conventions.convention: The signed difference is D=A−B; positive population bias means A reads larger than B on average.

The measurement conditions and target population have a declared probability law. D is square-integrable; its bias and standard deviation are finite. Scientific applicability is assumed rather than established.

Conventional limits use the rounded multiplier 1.96. Sample plug-in limits assume iid differences and n≥2, and use sample variance with denominator n−1. They assert no endpoint confidence coverage or exact finite-sample coverage.
For 0<p<1, the lower p-quantile is inf{x:F_D(x)≥p}. Under AC and an exact normal law, the exact multiplier is the unique z with Φ(z)=0.975.
The central interval is closed. Its probability is 0.95 when σ_D>0; when σ_D=0 both quantiles equal μ_D and the singleton has probability 1.
The repeated-measures example uses eight equally likely triples, three independent Rademacher coordinates, and differences D_j=U+ε_j for j=1,2.

load_bearing.statement: Assume the paired difference D:=A−B is square-integrable. Define population bias μ_D:=E[D] and standard deviation σ_D:=sqrt(Var(D)). The conventional rounded normal-reference limits of agreement are μ_D−1.96σ_D and μ_D+1.96σ_D.

published_dependencies.used_for: Measurable real-valued measurements on a common probability space.
The iid sample convention and the conclusion that dependent repeated differences are not iid.
Population expectations as Lebesgue integrals.
Bias, variance, standard deviation, and centered-product covariance.
Measurability of differences, centered differences, and absolute values.
Measurability of the centered square defining variance.
Moment bounds and upper and lower bounds on normal probability increments.
Finite integrability bounds establishing well-defined population bias and variance.
Existence and uniqueness of the finite nonnegative standard deviation.
The normal density, affine pushforward law, and zero-variance Dirac case under AC.
Positivity, measurability, and normalization of the standard normal density.
Probability subtraction, complements, and continuity for normal tail limits.
The countable-choice hypothesis supplied by AC for the measure and integral interfaces.
The explicit normal-law hypothesis and its implication of countable choice.
Singleton nullity and interval lengths in the normal CDF argument.
The standard normal law has no atoms.
Positivity of the exponential in normal density bounds.
Continuity and differentiation of the exponential.
Monotonicity of the exponential and hence explicit positive density bounds on compact intervals.
Reflection of compact normal-density integrals using the differentiable map t↦−t with constant integrable derivative.
Bounded Riemann integrability of the continuous density on compact intervals.
Identification of compact Riemann and Lebesgue integrals before applying reflection and probability tail limits.
Existence of the standard normal 0.975 quantile on a finite closed interval.
Covariance with a constant and expansion of random-intercept covariance and variances.
Explicit moments on the two-point and eight-point probability spaces.
Coordinate independence and the event-factorization test for dependence.
Vanishing cross covariances between distinct independent coordinates.
